summary: Specifies requirements and PCEP protocol extensions for global concurrent optimization, where the paths of a set of traffic engineering label switched paths are computed or reoptimized together rather than one by one.

plainLanguage.summary: Planning every route at once usually gives better results than planning one at a time. This note adds ways for the route server to do that.

subtitle: PCEP extensions for computing or reoptimizing a whole set of traffic engineering paths together instead of one by one.

tldr.problem: Computing TE LSP routes one at a time can fragment network resources and block later requests, and reoptimizing paths one by one may give little network-wide gain.
tldr.mechanism: PCEP requests can bundle many path computations using the SVEC object, add an objective function and a new Global Constraints object, and ask for an ordered reply (new D and M flags, Order TLV) that tells how to migrate without disruption.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the requirements, the new flags, TLV, object and error codes. It leaves the optimization algorithms out of scope and recommends the feature mainly for stable networks driven by a management system.

today: RFC 5557 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds directly on RFC 5440 and defines extensions, not the optimization algorithms themselves.

sections.title: Why Optimize Paths Together
sections.content:
The PCE architecture (RFC 4655) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC), such as a router or a Network Management System (NMS), ask a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute Traffic Engineering LSPs using PCEP. RFC 5557 adds requirements and extensions for Global Concurrent Optimization (GCO): computing a set of TE paths concurrently so network resources are used efficiently.

As LSPs come and go, network resources become fragmented. A GCO can look at the whole topology and the complete set of LSPs with their constraints, or at a subset of them. The algorithms are out of scope. GCO is described as primarily an NMS or PCE-server solution, and distributed alternatives with complex synchronization are NOT RECOMMENDED.

It is also NOT RECOMMENDED for networks with a very large number of very low or zero bandwidth LSPs, or with a high rate of LSP change. It suits stable networks such as transport networks. The RFC contrasts it with Backward Recursive PCE-based Computation (RFC 5441), which computes one shortest constrained inter-domain path.
sections.plainLanguage: Fitting suitcases into a car works better if you pack them all together rather than one after another. But if people keep adding and removing bags, the plan gets stale. So this is best for steady situations.

sections.title: Where GCO Applies
sections.content:
In the architecture, an NMS plays the PCC. It receives an application request, for example a traffic demand matrix, and asks the PCE for a global concurrent computation. The PCE returns the paths and the NMS gives head-end LSRs a fully computed explicit path for each LSP.

  • Greenfield optimization: no TE LSPs exist yet. A one-time optimization lets a planner provision a set of LSPs without blocking. It applies to single-layer and multi-layer networks.
  • Reoptimization: existing LSPs use resources poorly. Computing one LSP at a time can give little network-wide improvement in loaded networks with large LSPs. GCO can also help after catastrophic failures, avoiding races between head-end LSRs, though a centralized system typically responds more slowly.
  • Traffic migration: moving to the new set should avoid disruption. Make-before-break may be impossible if resources cannot hold both sets, so the PCE may order replacements or use temporary paths.

Traffic disruption may be acceptable for low priority services such as Internet traffic, but not for mission critical ones such as voice.
sections.plainLanguage: You can plan a brand new town all at once, or rearrange a busy town. Rearranging means moving traffic in a careful order so nobody gets stuck.

sections.title: What PCEP Must Be Able to Say
sections.content:
The RFC lists capabilities PCEP SHOULD support, built on the generic requirements of RFC 4657:

  • An indicator that a request is a global concurrent computation.
  • A Global Objective Function, with at least: Minimize aggregate Bandwidth Consumption (MBC), Minimize the load of the Most Loaded Link (MLL), and Minimize Cumulative Cost of a set of paths (MCC).
  • Global constraints: maximum and minimum link utilization, an overbooking factor, a maximum hop count, exclusion of links or nodes, and an indication that more reoptimization may become possible once traffic has moved.
  • A way to list all the concurrent requests. The existing SVEC object of RFC 5440 already does this.
  • Failure reasons such as no feasible solution, memory overflow, PCE too busy, PCE not capable, no migration path, or administrative privileges not allowing it.

To limit disruption, the request MUST be able to ask for ordering, the PCE MUST be able to report the order, and each request MUST be able to say whether make-before-break is required or break-before-make is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: Before building the tool, the authors wrote a shopping list of what the planner must be able to be told and what it must be able to answer.

sections.title: Request Message Changes
sections.content:
The PCReq message keeps the shape of RFC 5440, but the svec-list now allows three optional objects after each SVEC: the Objective Function (OF, from RFC 5541), the new Global Constraints (GC), and the eXclude Route Object (XRO, from RFC 5521).

A request is marked as GCO implicitly: if an OF, GC or XRO follows the SVEC, all path computations in that SVEC are subject to it. The global objective functions use OF function codes 4 (MBC), 5 (MLL) and 6 (MCC).
sections.plainLanguage: The request form gets a few optional boxes after the list of jobs. Filling them in tells the planner to apply those rules to every job in the list.

sections.title: Ordering the Migration
sections.content:
Two new flags go in the RP object: the M-bit (bit 21), meaning make-before-break is required, and the D-bit (bit 22), meaning the PCC requires the reply to report the order of this request. When M is not set, break-before-make is allowed. M can be set only if the R (Reoptimization) flag is set.

If D was set, the PCE MUST include an Order TLV (type 5) in the RP object of the PCRep. It holds a 32-bit Delete Order for removing the old LSP and a 32-bit Setup Order for setting up the new one. They SHOULD NOT be equal. A delete order higher than the setup order means make-before-break is possible. A delete order of 0 means the LSP is new.

In the RFC's example, R1 has remove order 1 and setup order 4, and R2 has remove order 3 and setup order 2. The NMS removes P1, sets up P2', removes P2, then sets up P1'. So R1 is reoptimized break-before-make and R2 make-before-break.
sections.plainLanguage: The planner hands out numbered steps. If an old road is closed after the new road opens, nobody is stranded. If it is closed first, there is a gap.

sections.title: The Global Constraints Object
sections.content:
The GC object (Object-Class 24, Object-Type 1) carries limits for all computations in a GCO request. Its body has four 8-bit fields followed by optional TLVs, though none are defined in this document.

  • MH: maximum hop count for all LSPs.
  • MU: upper-bound link utilization percentage, between 0 and 100.
  • mU: lower-bound utilization percentage, between 0 and 100.
  • OB: overbooking percentage. For example, 10% means 110 Mbps can be reserved on a 100 Mbps link.

Excluding nodes or links from the whole computation is done by placing an XRO after the GC object in the SVEC list.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a rules card that applies to every route in the batch: not too many stops, not too crowded, not too empty, and how much extra booking is allowed.

sections.title: Errors and No-Path Reasons
sections.content:
A PCE sends a PCErr with new Error-Type 15 when it cannot handle a GCO request. Error-value 1 means insufficient memory. Error-value 2 means it is not capable of GCO. A policy refusal uses the existing Error-Type 5 with new Error-value 5, global concurrent optimization not allowed. In each case the PCE stops processing and the request MUST be cancelled at the PCC.

When no solution is found, the NO-PATH object in the PCRep can carry two new flags in its NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV: no migration path found, and no feasible solution meeting all GCO constraints. A new PCE-CAP-FLAGS value 9 lets PCE discovery advertise GCO capability.
sections.plainLanguage: If the planner runs out of memory, is not able to do this job, or is not allowed to, it sends a short note saying which. If no plan fits, it says why.

sections.title: Security and Operations
sections.content:
Applying global reoptimization to an active network could be extremely disruptive. If wrong results reach the NMS, wrong actions may be taken. The operator issuing the commands must have sufficient authority and be authenticated, and the request must be subject to policy. The PCEP session security of RFC 5440 can protect the requests and responses.

For manageability, a PCC implementation SHOULD be able to configure whether it may send GCO requests. A PCE SHOULD be able to configure GCO support, the maximum number of synchronized path requests per request message, and GCO-specific policies such as authorized senders and request rate limiting.
sections.plainLanguage: Rearranging every road at once is risky, so only trusted people should be allowed to ask, and the planner can limit how big a batch it will accept.
